title: Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation for Network Configuration Safety
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) to measure the effect of a deterministic network‑configuration validator plus an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini (hosted adapter openai_responses) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on N = 200 paired intents (completed_episode_count = 400; model_calls_used = 200), every shared initial candidate passed validator checks so no repairs were attempted or applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Observed outcomes: baseline_success = 200/200, guarded_success = 200/200; paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. We present artifact‑grounded methodology, execution accounting, representative validator diagnostics, and a focused discussion clarifying the causal limits of the executed estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics and preregistered follow‑on designs required to measure repair efficacy under independent sampling or adversarial conditions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for intent→configuration workflows in network operations (NetOps). Translating operator intent into multi‑step device configuration sequences is operationally sensitive: syntactic mistakes, incorrect sequences, or fabricated fields can cause redundancy loss, policy violations, or service disruption if applied to devices. A common architectural mitigation is a generate→validate→repair (GVR) pipeline: generate candidate configuration(s), apply a deterministic validator to detect violations against intent and topology constraints, then trigger automated repair only when the validator detects a fault. Prior literature documents verifier‑guided feedback improving correctness in adjacent domains such as infrastructure‑as‑code and program repair [3], and recommends grounding and retrieval strategies to reduce hallucination in operational text tasks [1],[2]. However, empirical transfer of verifier‑guided pipelines to execution‑level NetOps safety (that is, whether generated configuration sequences would be unsafe when executed) remains an open question [4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment that intentionally implements a narrowly defined estimand: shared_initial_candidate semantics. For each intent, exactly one sampled initial generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline (no validator or repair applied) and guarded (validator applied; at most one automated repair permitted) episodes. Under these semantics any paired difference can only arise from deterministic validation and any subsequent permitted repair of that identical candidate. Our research question is therefore precisely: under shared_initial_candidate semantics, does permitting a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair change the proportion of validator‑valid executable configurations relative to leaving the same initial candidate unguarded? The contribution is threefold: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of the executed paired experiment (N = 200 pairs) with validator traces and deterministic reconciliation; (2) exact numeric inferential results and representative diagnostics explaining why repairs did not execute; (3) preregistered, artifact‑supported follow‑on estimand variants and concrete design recommendations required to measure repair efficacy under independent sampling, increased difficulty, or adversarial inputs.
sections.related_work:
Broad surveys and empirical reports document hallucination and reliability problems for LLM outputs and motivate grounding, retrieval, and verification strategies for operational tasks [1]. Retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded pipelines can reduce hallucination in operations‑style question answering and documentation tasks, though those evaluations typically focus on textual fidelity rather than device‑level executability [2]. Generate→verify→repair architectures have shown improvements in related code/IaC domains (for example, verifier‑guided fine‑tuning and policy‑guided repairs) and directly motivated our GVR design [3]. Recent NetOps capability studies highlight LLM strengths and limits for intent translation but emphasize capability metrics rather than execution‑level safety measures that map generated commands to executable device states in simulators or emulators [4]. Comprehensive AIOps surveys contextualize these directions and call for execution‑aware benchmarks and higher‑fidelity validators to bridge model outputs to operational safety [5].

The verified literature therefore supports two methodological gaps that shaped our design. First, verifier‑guided demonstrations improve code/IaC correctness but do not measure whether corrections prevent unsafe executable states when enacted on networks; transferability to NetOps remains an empirical question. Second, prior work rarely isolates the causal contribution of a validator/repair acting on the same generator output; shared_initial_candidate semantics explicitly separate downstream validator/repair effects from sampling variability in the generator.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered before any model calls (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01). The primary estimand is the paired difference in the proportion of validator‑valid executable configurations between guarded and baseline conditions under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The confirmatory hypothesis H1 stated that the GVR pipeline (validator + ≤1 repair) reduces executable unsafe configurations relative to baseline on the same sampled candidate. The preregistration fixed task_count = 200 pairs (planned_episode_count = 400), generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Analysis plan specified an exact two‑sided McNemar test for the primary confirmatory hypothesis and a paired bootstrap (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) for a 95% percentile CI.

Task generation, contamination checks, and difficulty annotations. A deterministic task generator produced the manifest of 200 synthetic "intent_configuration_repair_v1" tasks. Each manifest entry records initial_state, required_sequence, explicit workflow_policies, and difficulty annotations (e.g., "safe_access_service_transfer", "rolling_access_vlan_migration", "extreme" pattern labels). The preregistered contamination_plan ran SHA‑256 exact‑match checks and n‑gram similarity tests against repair and background corpora before any model calls; no exact‑match exclusions were detected and the confirmatory sample executed intact. The execution_bundle includes execution/task_manifest.jsonl and analysis/contamination_summary.csv documenting these checks.

Generator, sampling semantics, and provider audit. The declared generator was gpt‑5‑mini via the hosted adapter openai_responses. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" and temperature = null/unset; the preregistration and Methods explicitly state that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Provider audit traces (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json) record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, consistent with exactly one shared initial generation per pair. These traces are available under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/responses/ in the evidence bundle.

Deterministic validator and permitted repair. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation." The validator parses candidate command sequences, checks workflow and group constraints, and emits a structured trace containing validation_before and validation_after subtables with parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, violation_codes, repair_applied flag, and a boolean validator.valid. For guarded episodes the pipeline was permitted at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics only the guarded arm could alter the identical initial candidate via repair; baseline reused the same candidate unchanged. The validator outputs and per‑episode JSON scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) were the source for all binary outcome labels and repair counters used in analysis.

Outcome mapping and missingness. Each episode's boolean outcome was mapped directly from validator.valid to a binary "executable/valid" label for analysis. The primary missingness treatment followed the preregistered complete_pair_primary rule (exclude incomplete pairs). A sensitivity analysis was preregistered to treat missing or failed episodes as unsafe ('failure‑as‑zero'). In practice the execution produced no missing or failed episodes; analysis/missingness_summary.csv documents complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed episodes.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed according to the preregistered plan: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200. Deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms complete_pair_count = 200 and consistency across episode, pair, and provider accounting. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, consistent with the preregistered shared sampling semantics.

Primary outcomes and inferential statistics. Analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline_successes = 200/200 and guarded_successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 per condition). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) for the paired difference is [0.0, 0.0]. These numeric artifacts are archived and referenced by analysis/results.json.

Repair activity and representative validator diagnostics. Across the confirmatory sample repair_attempt_count = 0 and repair_applied_count = 0: the validator flagged no violations on any shared initial candidate, so the guarded pipeline never invoked the permitted repair path. Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (for example, execution/scoring/task‑000004‑baseline.json and task‑000004‑guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and identical validation_after.normalized_configuration. Example excerpt (task‑000004 shared_initial_candidate):

interface edge2 admin down
interface edge2 vlan 40
interface edge2 admin up
interface edge1 admin down

For this task parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and validator.valid = true; validator.violation_count = 0 and repair_applied = false. Similar diagnostics appear in the archived artifacts for task‑000005, task‑000006, and other representative items. The artifacts used for these summaries are execution/scoring/*.json and execution/responses/*.txt; representative artifact hashes are recorded in the execution manifest.

Compact repair summary table (artifact‑grounded). The preregistered reviewer request for an explicit repair summary is answered directly from the archived scoring artifacts and the analysis/condition_summary.csv: total_pairs = 200; repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0. (See analysis/condition_summary.csv and execution/scoring/ for the per‑episode sources.)

Contamination and failure accounting. Preexecution contamination checks flagged no exact matches; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. There were no infrastructure failures or retrials; execution_manifest.completed_episode_count = 400 and failed_episode_count = 0. Deterministic_reconciliation reports all consistency checks passed. These artifacts support the transparency of the null pathway: the guarded pipeline could not change any outcomes because the validator did not detect any violations on the shared sampled candidates.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and causal scope. The shared_initial_candidate semantics deliberately isolate the causal channel of interest: the validator and permitted repair acting on an identical sampled candidate. The executed estimand therefore answers only whether deterministic validation and a single permitted automated repair can change the validator‑valid label when confronted with the exact same generator output. The null result (paired difference = 0.0 with CI [0.0,0.0]) demonstrates that, for this task bank and single sampled candidate per intent, the validator observed no faults to act upon and therefore the guarded path lacked opportunity to alter outcomes.

Why repairs did not run. Artifact diagnostics show a consistent pattern: normalized_configuration from the shared initial candidate equaled the task's required_sequence and satisfied workflow_policies in validation_before for every pair (parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and violation_count = 0). Because the validator's decision rule is deterministic and maps to a boolean valid flag, no guarded repair attempts were permitted by policy when validator.valid = true. This chain of evidence — per‑episode validator traces, matched parsed/required command counts, and empty violation lists — is recorded in execution/scoring/*.json and explains the degenerate contingency.

Threats to validity and construct limits (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the paired shared_initial_candidate design eliminates cross‑condition sampling variability and therefore attributes any paired difference to downstream validation/repair only. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic, sequence, and workflow policies but does not execute vendor CLI or perform packet‑level emulation; dynamic runtime behaviors and timing interactions are therefore not represented in the validator's abstraction. External validity: a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini via openai_responses), a synthetic deterministic task bank, and a single validator implementation were used; generalization beyond these artifacts is unsupported. Conclusion validity: the absence of discordant pairs prevents inference about repair benefit magnitude under different sampling regimes because the repair path was never exercised.

Concrete, artifact‑supported follow‑on designs. Given the archived evidence, four preregistered modifications would enable empirical measurement of repair efficacy under operationally realistic regimes: (A) remove shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded arms receive independent first‑pass samples (this permits repair to act on generator faults but requires revised paired analysis to separate sampling variability from repair effects); (B) select or synthesize tasks labeled with "extreme" difficulty or inject adversarial perturbations to raise expected validator failure rates and thereby exercise repairs; (C) preregister explicit non‑null temperature sweeps in model_configuration.json to control sampling diversity and observe validator‑failure tradeoffs; (D) increase validator fidelity by integrating vendor CLI semantics and packet‑level emulation so repairs are judged against dynamic runtime behavior rather than static intent constraints. Each change is implementable using the archived task generator, provider audit procedures, and validator interface artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment designed to measure the downstream effect of a deterministic validator plus an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on 200 paired intents, every shared initial candidate passed validation and no repairs were attempted or applied; guarded and baseline outcomes were identical for the executed estimand (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This artifact‑grounded null result demonstrates an estimand boundary: under shared_initial_candidate semantics and the executed task bank the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to change outcomes. It does not imply that GVR pipelines are unnecessary generally. To evaluate repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability and adversarial conditions, preregistered follow‑on experiments that (1) remove shared_initial_candidate semantics, (2) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial inputs, (3) set explicit sampling parameters, and (4) raise validator fidelity are required. Finally, to avoid reader confusion we reiterate explicitly: the preregistered primary estimand was intentionally limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics; independent per‑condition sampling would constitute a different, separately preregistered estimand and experimental design.

After the autonomy lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01), code generation, execution, deterministic validation, automated analysis, and manuscript drafting without manual human editing of technical content. Declared model used in execution: gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution used model_calls_used = 200; archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Generation semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored candidates using 'full_intent_constraint_validation' and a single automated repair iteration was permitted in guarded episodes; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired intents) completed without preregistration deviations. Master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt — SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence in this final run. After the autonomy lock no human manually rewrote technical results, manuscript text, figures, or references.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design produced exactly one sampled initial generation per intent and reused it across baseline and guarded conditions; this measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature = null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is an abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task bank and sampling semantics rather than evidence that GVR is unnecessary in general.
